topic: diagnosing reversed composition and unverified inverse domains

traps.desc: applied the two rules in the reverse order, computing g(f(6)) instead of f(g(6))

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response says the two rules were applied in the wrong order -- the inner rule g must act on the input first, and only then does f act on that output. Full credit names which rule was used first (f) and which should have been (g), or equivalently says that the value -2 is g(f(6)) rather than f(g(6)). Saying only 'arithmetic mistake' or 'wrong answer' earns no credit.

traps.desc: assumed the square root always returns the original input, so the round trip gives -3 back

problems.desc: Part (b): the round trip returns 3, not the -3 it started from, so the claimed rule is not an inverse on all inputs. A correct response says that squaring destroys the sign, so two different inputs share one output and no rule can send that output back to both; the claimed rule can only work once the inputs are restricted (for example to values that are not negative). Full credit needs the round trip failing AND the reason (two inputs, one output / not one-to-one).

traps.desc: squared the input first and subtracted 4 afterwards, which is the other composition

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response says the subtraction has to happen before the squaring, because the inner rule acts first -- the written rule squares first and so is the other composition. Full credit refers to the order of the two rules, not just to the different numbers; a response that only reports 9 against 45 without naming the order has not diagnosed anything.

Part (b): the inverse rule has to carry the restriction that its inputs are at least 3, because the outputs of the original rule are never below 3 (a square root is never negative, and 3 is added to it). A correct response states that restriction and ties it to the range of the original rule. Noting that the squaring rule alone would happily accept an input like 1 and return an output the original never produced is the strongest form of the argument.

traps.desc: flipped the numerator and denominator of the original rule instead of solving for the input

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response says that swapping numerator and denominator produces the reciprocal of the rule, not its inverse -- the reciprocal undoes multiplication, while an inverse undoes the whole rule and must be found by solving for the input. Full credit distinguishes reciprocal from inverse, or shows that composing the claimed rule with the original does not return the input.

Part (c): a correct response explains that setting the two composed rules equal leaves a linear equation once the squared terms cancel, and a linear equation has exactly one solution -- so the two compositions can agree at one input and nowhere else. Full credit needs the cancellation of the squared terms (or an equivalent argument that the difference of the two rules is linear and not constant); simply asserting 'they are different functions' is not a reason.
